abstract: To investigate the mechanism of yeast fermentation on the evolution of taste substances of Jinhua ham, the effects of Rhodotorula mucilaginosa (B2, S13 and S38) and Candida parapsilosis (B10) fermentation on structural protein degradation, taste components and sensory characteristics were studied. The scores of aftertaste-A, aftertaste-B and richness showed the highest scores in S13 group among these treatments (B2, S13, S38, B10 and control group), and higher proteolytic enzyme and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities observed in S13 group contributed to the more intense degradation of myosin. The peptides derived from MYH7B and MYH1 accounted for 58.06 % of the total peptides, and 25 oligopeptides showed kokumi potential. 1 H NMR indicated that 15 free amino acids and 5 γ-glutamyl peptides showed higher contents in S13 group compared with other groups. PLSR and correlation network analysis demonstrated that the accumulation of free amino acids and oligopeptides was responsible for taste enhancement of Jinhua ham.

2
Materials and methods
2.1
Preparation of yeast and sampling of Jinhua ham
The preparation of yeast was conducted following the description of (
Simoncini et al., 2015
). The strains of
Rhodotorula mucilaginosa
(B2, S13 and S38) and
Candida parapsilosis
(B10) were isolated from the edible part of Jinhua ham, and no potential toxicological risks were found when the yeast sequences were compared with the NCBI database.
Rhodotorula mucilaginosa
(B2, S13 and S38) and
Candida parapsilosis
(B10) were activated on YPD medium at 28 °C. The concentration of the yeast suspensions was adjusted to 10
6
CFU/mL using physiological saline through spectrophotometric analysis and stored at 4 °C prior to inoculation.
The raw legs were salted with 60 g NaCl, 0.15 g NaNO
2
and 0.15 g KNO
3
per kilogram of raw legs. When no salt was visible on the ham surface, the ham samples were stored at 0–4 °C with a relative humidity of 75–85 % for 40 d, allowing them to reach salt equilibrium. After salt equilibrium, the ham surfaces were washed and air-dried to obtain ham samples. Fifty ham samples were randomly allocated into five groups, and yeast suspensions of
Rhodotorula mucilaginosa
(B2, S13 and S38) or
Candida parapsilosis
(B10) were inoculated onto the ham samples using a sprayer, following the methodology described by
Zhang et al. (2025)
to achieve an initial microbial load of 10
6
CFU/kg; the inoculation counts of the yeast were confirmed by the analysis of high-throughput sequencing and total fungal counts. These samples that were inoculated with
Rhodotorula mucilaginosa
(B2, S13 and S38) or
Candida parapsilosis
(B10) were defined as B2 group, S13 group, S38 group and B10 group, respectively. The samples were not inoculated with yeast which were defined as the control group (CK). To ensure the reliability and consistency of fermentation, the five groups of ham samples were fermented in separate dry-ripening rooms, where the temperature and relative humidity of each dry-ripening room individually controlled by an automatic control unit. The fermentation of five groups was carried out simultaneously according to the program setting. The ham samples of five groups (B2, S13, S38, B10 and CK) were fermented for a total of 80 days under the same conditions as described by
Zhang et al. (2025)
; the fermentation procedures were set as 30 d at 20–25 °C and 70–85 % humidity, followed by 30 d at 25–30 °C and 65–75 % humidity, and finally 20 d at 20–25 °C and 60–80 % humidity. After the above dry-ripening process, the ham samples with a weight loss of 40–42 % were considered as the final products. Five ham samples were randomly collected and stored at −80 °C until subsequent research.
2.2
Electronic tongue analysis
The collection of water-soluble extracts and electronic tongue analysis were conducted following the description of
Liao et al. (2022)
. Briefly, 20 g samples with 80 mL of deionized water were homogenized at 10,000 rpm for 4 × 15 s using PTMR 2100 homogenizer (Kinematica, Littau, LU, Switzerland) and centrifuged at 8000
g
for 20 min. The water-soluble extracts were analyzed using a TS-5000Z taste sensor (Insent Inc., Japan). The taste intensity was measured and converted into numerical values via taste analysis software. The average values of three repetitions in each group were recorded.
2.3
The preparation of crude enzyme solution
Following the description of
Li et al. (2025)
, crude enzyme solution of Jinhua ham samples was prepared. Briefly, 5 g samples were suspended in 30 mL sodium phosphate buffer (50 mM, pH 7.5) with 5 mM EGTA. The mixture was homogenized at 10, 000 rpm for 4 × 15 s and subsequently centrifuged at 8000
g
for 2 min. Following filtration of the supernatant through a membrane filter, the filtrate was diluted using 50 mL sodium phosphate buffer (50 mM).
2.3.1
The determination of total proteolytic enzyme activities
The crude enzyme solution was placed in a 40 °C water bath for 2 min. 1 mL of crude enzyme solution and 1 mL of casein solution were mixed and reacted at 40 °C for 10 min. Then, 2 mL of trichloroacetic acid was added to terminate this reaction. For the control group, 2 mL of trichloroacetic acid and 1 mL of crude enzyme solution were reacted at 40 °C for 10 min before adding casein solution. The mixtures were placed for 10 min and then filtered through filter paper. 1 mL of filtrate, 1 mL of Folin reagent and 5 mL of sodium carbonate solution were mixed and heated in a 40 °C water bath for 20 min. At 680 nm, the absorbance was measured, and the entire procedure was performed in triplicate. The tyrosine standard curve was established by measuring the absorbance of a series of tyrosine standard solutions at 680 nm. The unit (U/g) of proteolytic enzyme activities was defined as the production of 1 μg of tyrosine per minute of casein hydrolysis.
2.3.2
The determination of γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities
The γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities assays were performed using a reaction system containing 0.6 mL of 50 mM boric acid‑sodium hydroxide buffer, 0.2 mL of 5 mM γ-GpNA and 0.2 mL of 20 mM Gly-Gly. Enzyme solution (0.2 mL) and the substrate mixture were mixed and placed in a water bath (37 °C) for 30 min. To terminate this reaction, 1 mL of 0.15 M hydrochloric acid was added. The absorbance was measured at 410 nm. The blank control was performed in the same conditions without Gly-Gly. The γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities were calculated based on the absorbance at 410 nm between experimental group and blank group. A standard curve was established by measuring the absorbance of various p-nitroaniline concentrations at 410 nm. The unit (U/g) of enzyme activities was defined as the release 1 μmol of p-nitroaniline from γ-GpNA per minute.
2.4
Proteolysis index (PI) analysis
The PI was measured following the description of
Zhou et al. (2019)
with some changes. Briefly, 1 g sample of Jinhua ham was homogenized with 10 mL of deionized water at 10,000 rpm for 4 × 15 s. Total protein contents of the ham extract were measured with a biuret reagent kit (Solarbio, Beijing, China). Subsequently, 100 μL of extracts and 400 μL of trichloroacetic acid (12.5 %) were added and shaken at 4 °C for 15 min; then the mixture was centrifuged at 2000
g
for 10 min. 2 M NaOH was added to adjust the pH of the supernatant (300 μL) to 9.0. Subsequently, 180 μL of 0.6 mg/mL fluorescamine (dissolved in acetone) was mixed with the solution and placed at 25 °C for 60 min in darkness. Under the conditions of λex = 375 nm and λem = 475 nm, the fluorescence intensity of the mixtures was measured. Glycine standard curve was drawn with different concentrations of glycine standard solutions. PI was defined as the ratio of N-terminal α-amino contents to total protein contents in the samples.
2.5
The analysis of SDS-PAGE
The extraction of myofibrillar proteins and SDS-PAGE were performed following the operations of
Liao et al. (2022)
. Ham samples (5 g) were homogenized with 25 mL phosphate buffer (50 mM) with 1 mM EDTA at 10,000 rpm for 4 × 15 s using PTMR 2100 homogenizer (Kinematica, Littau, LU, Switzerland) and centrifuged at 8000
g
for 20 min. Then, the pellets were redissolved in 25 mL phosphate buffer (50 mM). The above procedures were repeated three times, and the remaining pellets were identified as myofibrillar protein. The contents of above proteins were measured using Biuret assay kit. To evaluate the degradation of myofibrillar proteins, SDS-PAGE was performed using a 12 % polyacrylamide separation gel and a 5 % polyacrylamide stacking gel. After the gel was stained and destained, the molecular weight of proteins was determined by reference to Color Mixed Protein Marker (10–250 kDa).
2.6
The extraction of the peptides
The extraction of peptides was carried out following the method of
Dai et al. (2024)
. Ham samples (20 g) were dissolved in 100 mL of 50 mM PBS and then homogenized for 4 × 15 s using PTMR 2100 homogenizer (Kinematica, Littau, LU, Switzerland) at 10,000 rpm. The homogenates were centrifuged at 10,000
g
for 15 min. Three volumes of ethanol were added to the supernatant standing for 24 h to remove the protein pellet. Subsequently, the supernatant was retained by centrifugation at 10,000
g
for 15 min. The ethanol was removed by vacuum evaporation and filtered through a 0.45 μm organic filter. The supernatant was ultrafiltered using 1 kDa ultrafiltration tube (Millipore). The collected filtrate was lyophilized in vacuum lyophilizer and stored at −80 °C.
2.7
Peptide separation by gel filtration chromatography
The gel filtration chromatography was conducted following the operations of
Dai et al. (2024)
with some changes. The lyophilized powder of peptides was dissolved in distilled water and filtered using 0.45 μm organic filter membrane. The peptides were separated by gel exclusion chromatography. Briefly, the solution was loaded onto a Sephadex G-15 gel filtration column (2 cm × 30 cm) that was filled with G-15 dextran gel. The loading volume was 1.5 mL and the concentrations were 6 mg/mL. Distilled water was used to elute the peptides at the flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. The detection was performed at 220 nm UV wavelength, and the fractions were collected using an automated fraction collector.
2.8
The identification of peptides by LC-MS/MS
The LC-MS/MS was carried out following the method of
Zhou et al. (2020)
. The F2 and F3 fractions separated from the gel column were mixed and lyophilized for LC-MS/MS analysis. The peptide powder was dissolved in Milli-Q water and reduced with DL-dithiothreitol (10 mM), following alkylation with iodoacetamide (50 mM) in darkness for 40 min. After desalting, the samples were reconstituted in 10 μL of formic acid (0.1 %) for LC-MS/MS. The nanoLC system, coupled with an Ultimate 3000 system, was equipped with a 150 μm × 15 cm in-house column packed with reversed-phase ReproSil-Pur C18-AQ resin (1.9 μm, 100 Å). Mass spectrometry analysis was performed using a Q Exactive™ Hybrid Quadrupole-Orbitrap™ Mass Spectrometer. The acquired MS/MS data were processed using Xcalibur software with the average local confidence threshold set at >90 % to ensure data reliability. The full scan range of mass spectrometry was set to 300–1800
m
/
z
. The mass resolution of the MS was set to 70,000, and the Maximum IT was set to 100 ms. The mass resolution of the MS/MS was set to 17,500, and the Maximum IT was set to 50 ms, while the collision energy for peptide fragmentation was set to 28. Amino acid sequences of the proteins were obtained by matching with UniProt databases.
2.9
The screening of kokumi peptides using deep learning
Screening kokumi peptides was conducted following the operations of
He et al. (2024)
with some changes. The SMILES structures of peptides were queried on the PubChem (version 2025,
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
). The SMILES format of the peptides was used to predict the kokumi intensity of the peptides using the algorithm of MorganFP-MLP on the deep-learning website (version 2024,
https://hwwlab.com/tastemeta/predmol
). Peptides with a predicted kokumi score closer to 1 exhibited higher kokumi intensity, thus peptides with kokumi intensity greater than 0.9 were screened for further analysis. Subsequently, the SMILES format of the peptide was imported into the web page (
http://www.swissadme.ch/
) to accept the number of rotatable bonds and hydrogen bond acceptors and the hydrophilicity and hydrophobicity of peptides. Peptides were screened based on the consensus Log P with an absolute value greater than 1. Peptides with kokumi score greater than 0.9, the absolute value of Log P greater than 1, and a high number of rotatable bonds and hydrogen bond acceptors were considered kokumi peptides.
2.10
1
H NMR spectroscopy
The
1
H NMR spectroscopy was conducted following the operations of
Zhou et al. (2021)
. 10 g ham samples were added to the methanol aqueous solution and the volume ratio of methanol to water was 2:1. The mixture was homogenized at 10,000 rpm for 3 min and centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 8 min. The methanol in the supernatant was removed by rotary evaporation and the remainder was freeze-dried. The lyophilized samples were re-dissolved in 600 μL of 0.15 M KH
2
PO
4
/Na
2
HPO
4
buffer (containing 50 % D
2
O and 0.1 % sodium 3-trimethylsilyl propionate) and centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 15 min. 500 μL of the supernatant was added to NMR tubes for NMR analysis. Metabolites were identified by the chemical shifts of the peaks using MestReNova (15.0.0). The contents of the metabolites were calculated based on the peak area ratio of sodium 3-trimethylsilyl propionate (internal standard) to the metabolites. The concentrations of the metabolites were calculated in triplicate, and the average values were used for subsequent analysis.
2.11
Statistical analysis
All results were expressed as the average ± standard deviation. The data of the total proteolytic activities, the γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities, PI, peptides and taste substances were analyzed using ANOVA at a significance level of 5 % by SPSS 24.0. PLSR was used to characterize the key metabolites by SMICA 14.1.

Introduction
Dry-cured ham is deeply loved by people for its unique organoleptic and taste. Kokumi contributes significantly to the formation of unique organoleptic and taste characteristics of dry-cured ham, which modifies the intensity of basic tastes including sweet, umami and salty, also provides a sensation of mouthfulness, thickness and richness to food. The key kokumi taste substances predominantly include free amino acids, small peptides, nucleotides and their derivatives (
Dashdorj et al., 2015
). The formation of these kokumi substances is largely governed by biochemical processes such as proteolysis in the fermentation stage of dry-cured ham (
Heres et al., 2023
). The proteolysis of dry-cured ham is generally mediated by endogenous enzymes and microbial activities during the fermentation of dry-cured ham (
Fu et al., 2022
). Several studies have emphasized the role of structural protein degradation by endogenous proteases in the formation of kokumi substances during the fermentation of dry-cured meat products. However, endogenous proteases are vulnerable to multiple factors including temperature, pH, relative humidity and fermentation duration, resulting in relatively inadequate activities in degrading proteins and developing the kokumi substances during the processing of dry-cured meat products (
Wu et al., 2024
). Notably, microorganisms can effectively make up for the deficiencies through their high activities and high environmental adaptability, and play a crucial role in protein degradation (
Kim & Kim, 2024
).
Wu et al. (2023)
reported that
Staphylococcus xylosus
and
Staphylococcus vitulinus
enhanced protein degradation, and promoted the accumulation of free amino acids and small peptides to improve overall acceptance and richness of the fermented bacon. The combination of
Tetragenococcus
and
Lentibacillus
enhanced the profile of glutamyl peptide and then contributed to kokumi attribute in a fermented fish product (
Phewpan et al., 2019
). Several studies have confirmed that bacteria show an improving effect on kokumi during fermented animal product processing. However, the roles of fungal microorganisms in the proteolysis of myofibrillar proteins and the formation of kokumi substances during dry-cured meat products processing remain relatively understudied. Yeast is a kind of the predominant fungi microorganisms during the fermentation-ripening of dry-cured ham, and the dominant microorganisms in dry-cured ham primarily include
Rhodotorula, Debaryomyces
,
Pichia, Yarrowia
and
Candida
(
Li et al., 2025
). Most of yeast could survive in high-salt and drought-tolerant environments, and play a key role in developing the taste substances and aroma of dry-cured meat products through improving proteolytic activities (
Zhang et al., 2025
).
Gong et al. (2023)
demonstrated that
Debaryomyces hansenii
was extensively used as an aroma enhancer to enhance the sensory properties of dry-cured ham. Furthermore, the promotion of protein degradation by yeast to produce bioactive peptides and flavor substances in dry-cured meat products has also been widely investigated (
Cai et al., 2022
). Several studies have found that extracellular proteases of yeast were insensitive to muscle protein degradation in vitro. Proteinase A and proteinase D isolated from the
Debaryomyces hansenii
CECT 12487 could accelerate proteolysis of myofibrillar proteins (
Bolumar et al., 2008
).
Rhodotorula mucilaginosa
AUMC 9298 and
Candida parapsilosis
d70a promoted the degradation of myosin and actin protein by their extracellular proteases activities to form small peptides and amino acids, improving the umami, aftertaste and richness (
Li et al., 2025
). Although these results indicated that yeasts showed great potential in degrading proteins by extracellular proteases to generate umami taste compounds, the underlying mechanisms of yeast-mediated kokumi substances evolution of dry-cured ham during the fermentation remain unexplored, and the key components responsible for the kokumi improvement and taste attributes have not yet been clearly identified and investigated during the fermentation of Jinhua ham. Therefore, it is great significance for the taste regulation of dry-cured ham to clarify the formation mechanism of yeast-mediated kokumi substances and the contribution of kokumi substances to taste.
LC-MS/MS and
1
H NMR are widely employed to identify taste compounds. LC-MS/MS showed the advantages of high throughput, precision and accuracy in identifying peptides and derivatives, but it is limited in detecting free amino acids (
Ewles & Goodwin, 2011
). Conversely, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) exhibits the advantages of non-destructive analysis and rapid qualitative and quantitative analysis of free amino acids and derivatives, but is constrained by complex NMR spectra of peptides in identifying peptides (
Cai et al., 2023
). Notably, the combination of LC-MS/MS and
1
H NMR facilitates a more comprehensive analysis of peptides and amino acids compared to either technique used individually. This complementary approach has demonstrated reliability in identifying peptides and free amino acids in several studies.
Windarsih et al. (2025)
employed
1
H NMR and LC-MS/MS to identify the taste components in beef sausages. A systematic analysis of bioactive components was also characterized in yellow onions using the approach of
1
H NMR and LC-MS/MS (
Soininen et al., 2012
). However, few studies pay close attention to characterizing the components and profiles of taste compounds using the combination of LC-MS/MS and
1
H NMR, and further investigating their effects on taste intensities of dry-cured ham fermented with different yeasts.
Therefore, the present research aimed to explore the roles of yeast inoculation on the cleavage changes of myofibrillar proteins and the evolution and profiles of taste substances of Jinhua ham using
1
H NMR and LC-MS/MS, and to further discuss the contribution of crucial components to kokumi development of Jinhua ham with different yeasts inoculation by PLSR and correlation network.

). The SMILES format of the peptides was used to predict the kokumi intensity of the peptides using the algorithm of MorganFP-MLP on the deep-learning website (version 2024,
https://hwwlab.com/tastemeta/predmol
). Peptides with a predicted kokumi score closer to 1 exhibited higher kokumi intensity, thus peptides with kokumi intensity greater than 0.9 were screened for further analysis. Subsequently, the SMILES format of the peptide was imported into the web page (
http://www.swissadme.ch/
) to accept the number of rotatable bonds and hydrogen bond acceptors and the hydrophilicity and hydrophobicity of peptides. Peptides were screened based on the consensus Log P with an absolute value greater than 1. Peptides with kokumi score greater than 0.9, the absolute value of Log P greater than 1, and a high number of rotatable bonds and hydrogen bond acceptors were considered kokumi peptides.
2.10
1
H NMR spectroscopy
The
1
H NMR spectroscopy was conducted following the operations of
Zhou et al. (2021)
. 10 g ham samples were added to the methanol aqueous solution and the volume ratio of methanol to water was 2:1. The mixture was homogenized at 10,000 rpm for 3 min and centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 8 min. The methanol in the supernatant was removed by rotary evaporation and the remainder was freeze-dried. The lyophilized samples were re-dissolved in 600 μL of 0.15 M KH
2
PO
4
/Na
2
HPO
4
buffer (containing 50 % D
2
O and 0.1 % sodium 3-trimethylsilyl propionate) and centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for 15 min. 500 μL of the supernatant was added to NMR tubes for NMR analysis. Metabolites were identified by the chemical shifts of the peaks using MestReNova (15.0.0). The contents of the metabolites were calculated based on the peak area ratio of sodium 3-trimethylsilyl propionate (internal standard) to the metabolites. The concentrations of the metabolites were calculated in triplicate, and the average values were used for subsequent analysis.
2.11
Statistical analysis
All results were expressed as the average ± standard deviation. The data of the total proteolytic activities, the γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities, PI, peptides and taste substances were analyzed using ANOVA at a significance level of 5 % by SPSS 24.0. PLSR was used to characterize the key metabolites by SMICA 14.1.
3
Results and discussion
3.1
Analysis of the electronic tongue of water-soluble substances of Jinhua ham
The results of electronic tongue of the extracted water-soluble substances from Jinhua ham with different yeasts fermentation are shown in
Fig. 1
A. The inoculation of B2, B10, S13 and S38 displayed markedly higher values in aftertaste and richness, while lower bitterness intensity was observed among these treatment groups (B2, B10, S13 and S38) in comparison with CK. Notably, compared with CK, the bitterness of samples that were inoculated with S13 decreased to 0.88 times, while the aftertaste-A and aftertaste-B scores increased to 1.72 and 2.38 times, and the richness scores increased to 1.15 times. These results suggested that the inoculation of S13 exhibited the most favorable taste among all groups. Aftertaste, richness, umami and bitterness are key indicators for evaluating the taste quality of meat products (
Wu et al., 2023
). Microorganism fermentation contributes to the development of unique taste substances by promoting protein degradation, and then enhances the taste attributes of fermented meat products (
Li et al., 2024
). Inoculation with
Staphylococcus vitulinus
and
Staphylococcus xylosus
on dry-cured bacon contributed to the enhancement of the aftertaste and umami, while the bitterness of the fermented bacon was reduced (
Zhou et al., 2024
).
Han et al. (2025)
demonstrated that inoculating
Tetragenococcus halophilus
2MH-3 into fermented fish sauce could increase the content of umami peptides and reduce bitterness. Compared with B2, B10, S38 and CK, S13 exhibited a higher ability to reduce bitterness in fermented meat products, which could be attributed to the formation of more kokumi substances under the action of S13, thereby masking the bitterness. In addition,
Rhodotorula mucilaginosa
AUMC 9298 exhibited higher extracellular proteases activities than
Candida parapsilosis
d70a during the fermentation process, and higher intensities of aftertaste, richness and umami were detected in samples inoculated with
Rhodotorula mucilaginosa
AUMC 9298 than those inoculated with
Candida parapsilosis
d70a (
Li et al., 2025
). In the present study, the highest scores of richness, aftertaste-A and aftertaste-B in these ham samples with the inoculation of S13 were observed compared with other yeast inoculation and CK, which might be due to the accumulation of taste substances including characteristic amino acids and peptides during the fermentation.

3.2
Total proteolytic activities and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities
Total proteolytic activities of Jinhua ham fermented with B2, B10, S13 and S38 are shown in
Fig. 1
B. The total proteolytic activities in B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK reached 11.74, 12.07, 13.77, 12.93 and 11.05 U/g. In the comparison with CK, the total proteolytic activities of the inoculation of B2, B10, S13 and S38 were significantly increased. Notably, the treatment of S13 exhibited the highest proteolytic activities among these groups (B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK). γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities of Jinhua ham fermented with B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK are shown in
Fig. 1
C. The γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities in B2, B10, S13 and S38 reached 0.23, 0.21, 0.28, 0.26 and 0.18 U/g. In the comparison with CK, the γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities of the inoculation of B2, B10, S13 and S38 were significantly increased. Notably, the treatment of S13 showed the highest γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities.
The above results indicated that the inoculation of S13 increased the proteolytic activities and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities of Jinhua ham. Proteolytic enzymes show a great potential to degrade muscle proteins into amino acids and peptides, which could influence the taste development of fermented meat products (
Wang, Li, et al., 2022
;
Wang, Xu, et al., 2022
). γ-glutamyl transpeptidase is capable of transferring γ-glutamyl groups to other amino acids or peptides, thereby synthesizing various γ-glutamyl compounds with specific taste functions (
Suzuki, 2021
). γ-glutamyl transpeptidase is considered the key enzyme for the formation of γ-glutamyl peptides through γ-glutamyl transfer and hydrolysis reactions during the processing of dry-cured ham (
Lu et al., 2021
).
Li et al. (2024)
demonstrated that
Penicillium chrysogenum
showed an intense hydrolytic ability for muscle protein, and the protease activities were 11.42 U/mL.
Li et al. (2020)
demonstrated that
Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
exhibited intense γ-glutamyl transpeptidase activities, which promoted the accumulation of γ-glutamyl peptides. Compared with
Penicillium chrysogenum
and
Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
, S13 exhibited higher ability to degrade proteins and produced amino acids and γ-glutamyl peptides, which could be attributed to differences in strains. In addition, the activities of proteolytic enzymes and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase during the production of dry-cured meat products are significantly influenced by various factors, such as the types of strains, temperature and pH, and the types of strains as a key factor influencing the activities of proteolytic enzymes and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase.
Debaryomyces marasmus
51 isolated from Parma ham has been proven to show an intense ability to adapt to the environment, which could live in an environment containing 3–5 % NaCl (
w
/w) and could enhance the extracellular proteases activities (
Simoncini et al., 2015
).
Penicillium nalgiovense
could survive within a wide range of water concentrations in dry-aged beef and enhance proteolytic activities (
Lee et al., 2022
). In this study, the highest protease activities in the treatment of S13 inoculation may be due to the strain of S13 showing a better adaptation during the fermentation conditions of Jinhua ham, which further accelerated the secretion of exogenous enzymes and then enhanced the activities of proteolytic enzymes and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase.
3.3
Proteolysis index (PI) and SDS-PAGE profile of myofibrillar proteins
Fig. 1
D shows the PI values of Jinhua ham samples fermented with B2, B10, S13 and S38. The PI values of the B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK were 24.75 %, 25.97 %, 28.69 %, 27.26 % and 18.25 %, respectively. The PI values of B2, B10, S13 and S38 markedly increased in comparison with CK, and the highest PI value was found in the samples inoculated with S13 among these groups (B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK). The SDS-PAGE profile of myofibrillar proteins of Jinhua ham samples fermented with B2, B10, S13 and S38 is presented in
Fig. 1
E. Compared with CK, myofibrillar proteins were degraded significantly in the inoculation of B2, B10, S13 and S38, and the most notable degradation of myofibrillar proteins occurred in the protein bands of 220 kD (possibly myosin heavy chain), 43 kD (possibly actin), 35 kD (possibly tropomyosin) and 32 kD (possibly troponin). These results indicated that the samples inoculated with S13 showed the greatest ability to promote protein hydrolysis of Jinhua ham.
Proteolysis plays a marked role in the production of amino acids and small-molecule peptides through the breakdown of myofibers during the fermentation of Jinhua ham (
Zhou et al., 2019
). PI is a crucial indicator to evaluate the degradation degree of myofibrillar proteins, and the PI values are highly associated with the activities of the inoculated microorganisms during the fermentation of dry-cured ham. A series of studies have demonstrated that inoculation with
Staphylococcus
,
Lactobacillus
and
Debaryomyces hansenii
promoted the protein hydrolysis of meat products by degrading characteristic structural proteins (
Gong et al., 2024
;
Wu et al., 2024
).
Staphylococcus carnosus
RT6 significantly degraded the proteins of myosin light chain by secreting extracellular proteases during the fermentation process of dry sausage (
Wang, Li, et al., 2022
;
Wang, Xu, et al., 2022
).
C. parapsilosis
d70a showed an intense ability to degrade actin in dry-cured ham. (
Li et al., 2025
). Compared with
Staphylococcus carnosus
RT6 and
C. parapsilosis
d70a, S13 significantly degraded the myosin heavy chains in Jinhua ham, which indicated that different strains showed the different ability to degrade myofibrillar proteins. In addition, the PI value increased to 1.05 times in air-dried goose inoculated with
Lactobacillus fermentum
for 5 days, while the PI value increased to 1.08 times in air-dried goose inoculated with
Staphylococcus epidermidis
for 5 days (
Wu et al., 2024
). In this study, PI value increased to 1.57 times in Jinhua ham inoculated with S13, which could be explained by the combined effect of long-term fermentation and good adaptability of the strain of S13 on the degradation of myosin heavy chain during the fermentation of dry-cured ham.

The proportions of F2 in B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK were 56.86 %, 58.60 %, 32.34 %, 30.29 % and 60.99 %, and the proportions of F3 in B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK were 24.92 %, 19.23 %, 47.04 %, 53.40 % and 21.14 %, respectively. 3.5
Cleavage sites of MYH7B and MYH1
In order to characterize the differences of peptide sequences between B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK, the cleavage sites of MYH7B and MYH1 were further analyzed. The potential cleavage sites for peptide release were annotated in MYH7B and MYH1 based on enzyme sites of Asp-N endopeptidase, Arg-C proteinase, glutamyl endopeptidase, Lys C, Lys N and Asp-N endopeptidase & N-terminal Glu in the UniProt database (
Zhou et al., 2020
), as shown in
Fig. 3
. Several high-intensity hydrolysis regions were observed in MYH1 at these positions of 1091–1110, 1201–1216, 1251–1280, 1310–1321, 1368–1378, 1141–1161 and 1867–1880, while the high-intensity hydrolysis regions of MYH7B were shown at these positions of 928–936 and 1149–1160. In terms of the N-terminal site, peptides EQIDNLQR and EVAQWR had an additional Glu with respect to peptides QIDNLQR and VAQW, while peptide QQIEELK showed an additional Gln with respect to peptide QIEELK in MYH1 observed in the ham samples with S13 inoculation. In terms of the N-terminal site, peptides AAVL and AYL had an additional Ala with respect to peptides AVL and YLM in MYH7B observed in the ham samples with S13 inoculation. In terms of the C-terminal site, peptide SELKTKE had an additional Glu with respect to peptide SELKTK, while peptide LQDLVDKLQ had an additional Gln with respect to peptide LVDKL observed from the degradation of MYH1 in the ham samples with S13 inoculation. In terms of the C-terminal site, peptide FA had an additional Ala with respect to peptide YF, which was observed from the degradation of MYH7B in the ham samples with S13 inoculation. Glu and Gln are key amino acids in the formation of γ-glutamyl peptides under the action of transpeptidase (
Mitrić & Castellano, 2023
).
Li et al. (2020)
demonstrated that a large number of Glu, Gln and Ala have been found in the composition of the currently identified kokumi peptides. These results indicated that a large amount of Glu and Gln were generated in Jinhua ham fermented with S13, which could provide sufficient substrates for the formation of γ-glutamyl peptides in the presence of γ-glutamyl transpeptidase and then enhance the kokumi intensity in Jinhua ham fermented with S13.

Five unique cleavage sites from MYH7B, including D-30, R-440, E-928, E-1158 and E-1496, and nine unique cleavage sites from MYH1, including D-1202, E-1209, E-1267, D-1276, Q-1314, E-1371, R-1376, D-1870 and Q-1876. Eleven common cleavage sites of L-14, W-29, P-38, R-246, F-425, F-516, P-544, H-580, W-597, Y-722 and V-996 were identified from MYH7B, and seven common cleavage sites of E-1121, E-1155, S-1203, L-1263, R-1272, K-1320 and N-1440 were identified from MYH1. In these unique cleavage sites of MYH7B and MYH1, E-1158, E-1496 and E-1209 were formed under the action of proteinase K, while E-928, E-1267 and E-1371 could be formed under the action of Glutamyl endopeptidase; the unique cleavage sites of R-440 and R-1376 could be formed under the action of Arg-C proteinase. Proteinase K showed an intense capacity to release amino acids from protein and small peptides (
Li et al., 2024
). Glutamyl endopeptidase can recognize Glu in the polypeptide chain and release it (
Nemoto et al., 2008
).
Wu et al. (2018)
indicated that Arg-C proteinase accelerated the digestion efficiency of protein to produce peptides and amino acids. These results indicated that protein can be degraded into amino acids and small peptides under the action of proteinase K, Glutamyl endopeptidase and Arg-C proteinase during the fermentation of Jinhua ham.

A, the distinct color distribution patterns intuitively reflect the differences in taste intensity and the number of bonds. As shown in Table S3, KCSS, KPEE, VASLNR, TAD, RRVK, GHT, AAQ, GRIDFD, AEELAE, TPGA, ISERLE, ELSERL, TVKG, VPN, AAH, GEKLK, VLDPE, VEGLR, KFEYGE, APKIPE, EGV, AH, VEDL, TVA and KPMG were selected according to the kokumi scores were more than 0.90 and the absolute values of consensus Log P were greater than 1. Notably, kokumi scores of RRVK, GRIDFD, TPGA, ISERLE, TVKG, VEGLR and KPMG were 1 and bitter scores were no more than 0.033. The number of rotatable bonds and hydrogen bond acceptors of ISERLE, ELSERL and KFEYGE were 32, 32 and 30, and 14, 14 and 14, respectively. ). A large amount of hydrophilic glutamic acid and aspartic acid are contained in γ-glutamyl peptides, which makes the peptide exhibit hydrophilicity (

). These results indicated that these peptides showed intense potential for kokumi.

Specifically, 42, 40, 45, 45 and 39 metabolites were identified in the treatment of B2, B10, S13, S38 and CK, respectively. It was worth noting that the concentrations of isoleucine, valine, alanine, arginine, tyrosine, phenylalanine, glutamic acid, methionine, tryptophan, serine, lysine, glutamine and glycine in B2, B10, S13 and S38 were higher than those in CK. The concentrations of γ-glutamyl peptides including γ-Glu-Ala, γ-Glu-Cys, γ-Glu-Gln, γ-Glu-Glu and γ-Glu-Lys in B2, B10, S13 and S38 were higher than those in CK. In
Fig. 5
C, the total contents of peptides and amino acids in S13 were higher than other groups. Notably, the highest concentrations of glutamine, glutamic acid and aspartic acid were found in S13, which were 1.76 mg/g, 9.31 mg/g and 3.36 mg/g, respectively. The highest concentrations of γ-Glu-Cys, γ-Glu-Ala, γ-Glu-Gln, γ-Glu-Lys and γ-Glu-Glu were also observed in S13, which were 5.89, 7.89, 12.23, 5.21 and 8.04 mg/g, respectively. Free amino acids are key contributors to taste, which play an essential role in the unique taste of dry-cured meat products (
Fu et al., 2022
). Glutamic acid, glutamine and aspartic acid contribute to kokumi and umami, while alanine and lysine belong to sweet amino acids (
Cai et al., 2023
). Furthermore, γ-glutamyl peptides containing γ-glutamyl residues contribute significantly to the kokumi taste in foods (
Li et al., 2025
). In this study, the highest contents of γ-glutamyl peptides and kokumi-enhancing amino acids including aspartic acid, glutamine and glutamic acid were observed in the ham samples with the inoculation of S13, which could be attributed to the inoculation of S13 showing the most potential to enhance the kokumi taste of the Jinhua ham.

4
Conclusion
The present study indicated that the aftertaste-A, aftertaste-B and richness scores in ham samples with S13 inoculation increased to 1.72, 2.38 and 1.15 times compared with CK. The highest activities of proteolytic enzymes (13.77 U/g) and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (0.28 U/g) were observed in the inoculation of S13, which primarily contributed to intense degradation of myosin and generation of taste substances. The results of LC-MS/MS and
1
H NMR spectroscopy further confirmed that S13 promoted the production of more peptides and taste substances compared with other groups. The degradation of MYH7B and MYH1 was mainly responsible for the accumulation of glutamic acid, serine, aspartic acid and arginine, which further accelerated the formation of AH, TVKG, γ-Glu-Gln, γ-Glu-Glu and γ-Glu-Cys. PLSR and correlation analysis further demonstrated that serine, aspartic acid, arginine, AH, TVKG, γ-Glu-Gln, γ-Glu-Glu and γ-Glu-Cys were the main contributors to enhanced richness and aftertaste of Jinhua ham. This study lays a foundation for subsequent study on exploring the kokumi perception pathway using cell models.
